item.title: Sebi confirms Rajesh Exports curbs, flags incomplete information in probe
item.description: Rajesh Mehta remains barred from dealing in Rajesh Exports securities as Sebi examines financial disclosures, subsidiary consolidation and alleged related-party fund routing.
item.dc:creator: Khushboo Tiwari
item.content:encoded: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Wednesday confirmed its interim directions against Rajesh Exports and its chairman, Rajesh Mehta, citing unresolved concerns over the company’s financial disclosures, consolidation of overseas subsidiaries and alleged routing of funds through related parties. The regulator also flagged several instances where information sought during its investigation remained outstanding or was submitted incompletely. Under the confirmatory order dated October 14, Mehta will continue to be restrained from buying, selling or otherwise dealing in the company’s securities, directly or indirectly, until further orders. “The material placed on record does not, at this stage, sufficiently eliminate the concerns that formed the basis of the interim order. The continuation of the directions is also proportionate to the nature of the concerns presently under investigation,” the order noted. Among its findings, Sebi noted that the difference between Rajesh Exports’ consolidated revenue of ₹15.45 trillion and Valcambi SA’s standalone revenue of ₹3,027.38 crore over the five-year period from 2020-21 to 2024-25 was about 99 per cent. The regulator said the company failed to provide a satisfactory reconciliation of the figures, adding that differences in reporting periods could not explain the disparity. Sebi also questioned a document submitted by the company to support its claim that Mehta had acted as a conduit for commodity trades on its behalf. Titled “Agreement for nominee facilitation of MCX trading and banking transactions,” the document was signed on behalf of the company by Managing Director Prashant Mehta. However, Sebi said it had received communications in which Prashant Mehta denied signing the document, including a statement shared by the Enforcement Directorate. The regulator said the document’s authenticity required further examination. It also noted that the company had not furnished board authorisation or explained the absence of related-party disclosures. The order reiterated concerns over the company’s disclosure of ₹1,035.27 crore as investments in gold mines in Africa, which Sebi said remained unsubstantiated by supporting documents. The regulator added that several information requests remained partially fulfilled or pending. These included details of import-export invoice adjustments, supporting correspondence and transactions between Mehta and counterparties, among others.

item.title: Housing demand up 8.2% in Q2FY27 on festive cheer: Magicbricks report
item.description: Magicbricks' PropIndex report showed housing demand rose 8.2 per cent in July-September 2026, with premium homes gaining traction, though demand stayed below year-ago levels ...
item.dc:creator: Akshat Ayush
item.content:encoded: India’s residential property market witnessed an improvement in buyer sentiment with the festive season in sight as housing demand rose 8.2 per cent between July and September 2026, according to Magicbricks’ PropIndex report. Major residential markets registered an increase in demand in Q2FY27 as property prices rose marginally. However, demand remained below year-ago levels. “The latest PropIndex findings reflect strengthening demand across key residential markets, alongside growing interest in premium housing. Homebuyers continue to prioritise location, space and value, while varying supply and price trends highlight the importance of local market dynamics,” Prasun Kumar, CMO at Magicbricks, said. Homes priced above ₹3 crore recorded notable demand growth in Greater Noida, Bengaluru and Noida. Magicbricks said this pointed to continued interest in higher-value properties, while also reflecting the varied nature of buyer demand, with premium housing gaining traction alongside sustained interest in more practical home configurations. Homebuyer preferences continued to centre on mid-sized homes, the report added. Properties measuring 750–1,250 square feet (sq ft) accounted for the largest share of demand, followed by homes in the 1,250–2,000 sq ft category. Together, these segments represented more than two-thirds of overall demand. Meanwhile, two-bedroom and three-bedroom apartments remained the most preferred configurations, highlighting buyers’ focus on balancing space requirements with location and overall value. On the supply side, active property listings registered a modest increase nationally, with Bengaluru recording the strongest growth among the highlighted markets, followed by Noida and Hyderabad. In contrast, available listings contracted in Gurugram, Chennai and Ahmedabad. Magicbricks said the variation in supply trends across cities indicated that market conditions continued to differ by geography, with some markets seeing an expansion in available inventory while others remained relatively constrained. Property prices continued to rise, with Mumbai and Chennai recording some of the strongest quarterly increases, followed by Ahmedabad and Bengaluru. Prices remained relatively stable in Greater Noida and Gurugram, reflecting differing demand-supply dynamics across residential markets.

item.title: Sebi proposes market cap-based SME listing norms, lower application size
item.description: Sebi proposes halving the minimum SME IPO application value to Rs 1 lakh, raising the operating profit threshold and easing offer-for-sale restrictions for institutional investors ...
item.dc:creator: Khushboo Tiwari
item.content:encoded: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Wednesday proposed an overhaul of the regulations around initial public offerings (IPOs) of small and medium enterprises (SMEs).  It plans to replace paid-up capital-based eligibility criteria with market capitalisation (mcap) thresholds, reduce the minimum application size to ₹1 lakh, and take measures to ease restrictions on offer-for-sale (OFS) by institutional investors. The regulator also proposed raising the minimum average operating profit requirement to ₹3 crore a year, while allowing established businesses that do not meet the profitability criterion to also access the market. However, it would be subject to certain criteria. In a consultation paper issued on Wednesday, Sebi proposed a broader overhaul of the SME IPO framework, including changes to promoter lock-in requirements, trading lots, underwriting and compulsory market making. The proposals seek to reduce the cost and compliance burden of raising capital, widen investor participation and align select requirements with those applicable to mainboard IPOs, while retaining safeguards for investors. Under the proposed eligibility framework, companies with post-issue mcap of up to ₹1,000 crore would be required to list on the SME platform. Those with mcap above ₹1,000 crore and up to ₹4,000 crore could opt for the SME platform. But they have to prepare their restated consolidated financial statements in accordance with Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) if they had not already adopted them. Sebi also proposed replacing the existing requirement of operating profit of at least ₹1 crore in two of the preceding three financial years with average operating profit of at least ₹3 crore a year over three preceding financial years, based on restated consolidated financial statements. However, companies that do not meet this profitability threshold could still undertake an IPO through the book-building route, provided at least 75 per cent of the net offer is allotted to qualified institutional buyers (QIBs). If the prescribed allocation is not achieved, the entire subscription money would have to be refunded. Other eligibility requirements relating to track record, business continuity and promoter stability would continue to apply. The regulator has proposed cutting the minimum application value by half from ₹2 lakh to ₹1 lakh. Each lot would have a minimum value of ₹25,000, requiring investors to apply for at least four lots. Separately, the trading lot for SME-listed securities would be reduced to one share, allowing investors greater flexibility in secondary-market transactions. On OFS, Sebi proposed a dedicated regulatory framework, including a one-year holding requirement for shares offered for sale, subject to specified exemptions. “We had specifically cautioned that raising application thresholds would exclude smaller investors. Sebi’s proposal to lower this barrier is an encouraging recognition of that concern. Removing the compulsory migration trigger linked to ₹25 crore paid-up capital also addresses an obstacle to continued fundraising by growing SMEs,” said Vinod Kumar, president, India SME Forum. The regulator has also proposed rationalising promoter lock-in requirements. The three-year lock-in for minimum promoters’ contribution would no longer be linked to the commencement of commercial production. Promoter holdings beyond the minimum contribution would be locked in for one year, replacing the existing staggered arrangement. The lock-in for pre-issue capital held by non-promoters would be reduced from one year to six months, while promoter group holdings would be subject to a one-year lock-in. Sebi further proposed removing the ₹10 crore absolute cap on the use of IPO proceeds for general corporate purposes, while retaining the limit of 15 per cent of the issue size. It also recommended changes to the underwriting and compulsory market-making framework as part of efforts to rationalise fundraising costs and SME-specific requirements. The SME platform has raised ₹40,222 crore since inception, with 365 companies migrating to the mainboard, according to Sebi data as of July 31, 2026. Sebi has sought comments from the public and stakeholders on the proposals by November 4.

item.title: US oil, gas supplies to India fall 43% as West Asia imports rebound
item.description: Refiners say high freight costs, longer voyages and limited supplies of medium sour crude make US barrels less attractive than West Asian and Russian alternatives ...
item.dc:creator: S Dinakar
item.content:encoded: West Asian producers led by the UAE, Iraq and Saudi Arabia will continue to be India’s leading energy suppliers once the war ends and cannot be replaced by the United States, three senior refining officials told Business Standard, as US oil and gas supplies fell sharply in September from this year’s high in May. Indian imports of crude oil, liquefied natural gas (LNG) and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) from the US declined 43 per cent in September to a combined 1.22 million tonnes from 2.13 million tonnes in August, marking the lowest level since April, according to ship-tracking data accessed by Business Standard. Despite the West Asia conflict disrupting India’s energy supplies since March and forcing Indian refiners to seek alternative sources, US oil and gas supplies fell marginally from September 2025. They also declined by more than half from a two-year high of 2.86 million tonnes in October 2025. In value terms, this translates into billions of dollars in reduced purchases. Imports of oil and gas from West Asia surged 67 per cent in September from August to 13.56 million tonnes, ship-tracking data accessed by Business Standard showed. October imports so far are close to 6 million tonnes and may exceed September’s purchases, according to projections by maritime intelligence agency Kpler. Gulf oil exports rebounded to roughly 16.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in September, near pre-war levels, despite only 60 per cent of those barrels crossing the Strait of Hormuz compared with 83 per cent before the war. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Iraq adapted through pipelines, bypass ports and extensive ship-to-ship transfers, trade journal OilPrice said, citing a note by Standard Chartered. Iran’s ability to choke off regional oil exports has consequently weakened, it added. Senior officials from state-run refiners said that while Washington was urging New Delhi to increase energy imports, the government had not issued any instructions on where to buy crude, LPG or LNG from. Economics remained the key consideration, they said. Record freight rates and limited supplies of medium sour crude grades from the US — the grades most suited to India’s complex refineries — have made imports of light sweet premium US crude less attractive to Indian refiners compared with Russian oil, the officials said. Crude oil imports from the US in October declined by around 30 per cent to 91,000 bpd compared with the whole of September, according to Kpler. Hiring rates for Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), which can carry around 2 million barrels of crude, have jumped more than 20-fold from pre-war levels to nearly $1.5 million a day from $50,000-$75,000 in early 2026, a shipbroker from Abu Dhabi told Business Standard. Transportation and insurance now constitute 20-25 per cent of the value of a crude consignment compared with less than 5 per cent before the war, two refining officials said.Trade agreement hiccupsThe sharp decline in crude imports comes even as India and the US face hurdles in concluding a bilateral trade agreement, where higher energy purchases are a key demand of US President Donald Trump.United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said signing a deal was not “imminent” because of a “universe of items that are sticking points”. Trump’s energy agenda has focused on policies enabling higher US oil and gas production while urging Europe, India, China and other Asian economies to buy more US energy as part of bilateral trade agreements. The European Union has stepped up purchases, with the US supplying a majority of its LNG and diesel. China also concluded a long-term LNG import contract during President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington this month. There has, however, been little progress in efforts by Indian state-run oil companies to conclude LNG or crude import deals with the US, with current purchases remaining “opportunistic”, a senior refining official said. Speaking at the Munich Security Conference this month, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said talks were still under way for an India-US trade deal. “Although we’d like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult. But maybe if there are room to operate from, both sides could do it,” she said. That room is slowly shrinking. Trump signed into law last month the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, giving him the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries, including India and China, that continue buying Russian oil and gas. Overall imports of US fossil fuels, excluding coal, exceeded 2 million tonnes three times in the past six months, with May supplies at 2.58 million tonnes, the second-highest in five years after 2.86 million tonnes in pre-war October 2025, Kpler data showed. But imports slowed considerably in September and October, the data showed. Besides high freight costs and travel times of more than 45 days from the US — with vessels detouring around the Horn of Africa to avoid Houthi attacks around the Suez Canal route — supplies of medium sour grades from West Asia have surged in recent weeks. That has benefited Indian refiners and reduced their need to buy from alternative sources.
